Article Title: Father sold apartment, quit job; mother pledged gold: The making of Sahithi Varshini, India's latest WGM
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: In May 2019, before the pandemic had pressed the pause button on the world, Sagar Shah, already an International Master (IM) and one of the most influential voices in today's chess fraternity, wrote a line in his ChessBase column: "Just like Humpy (Koneru) and Harika (Dronavalli) have made the world take note of Indian women's chess over the years, we have a feeling that within a few years Sahithi (Varshini Moogi) and Savitha (Shri Baskar) will also be right up there with the best in women's chess!"More than seven years have passed, and the same line reads less like a prediction and more like a question of legacy, much like asking whether Lamine Yamal could become the next Lionel Messi for Barcelona or whether Carlos Alcaraz could carry the torch of Spanish tennis after Rafael Nadal.Both girls are now 19. At the Chess Olympiad in Samarkand last month, Savitha added a team bronze to her growing list of accolades while also becoming the only Indian to win an individual gold medal at the event Sahithi Varshini, on the other hand, has had a less decorated career so far. The Vizag-born prodigy recently became India’s latest Woman Grandmaster (WGM), a milestone by any measure. But is this the best she can do?"Whatever she has achieved so far, including this one (the WGM title), is not up to her potential. This is just a mere beginning," Lokeswara Moogi Rao, her father and only coach to date, told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interaction.Just last month, Sahithi's third and final WGM norm came at the IM VII Round Robin in Serbia. The 2007-born player finished second with 6/9, recorded a performance rating of 2408, and gained 23 rating points. That completed the requirements.The first two norms came in Hungary. The first was achieved at the Golden Horse IM Round Robin in September 2025, while the second came at the Kanizsa Open in August 2026, where she defeated GM Yeshaayahu Tzidkiya and recorded a performance rating of 2429.On paper, it may look like a clean progression. But the story behind it is much messier.To give a glimpse of how challenging it has been, when Sahithi was six, she caught dengue. She was on a ventilator for a week. She survived, and her family has always seen her recovery as a second life.Long before chess became a part of his life, Lokeswara Moogi Rao, also known as Lokesh in the circuit, had discovered his passion in literature. During his college days, he spent hours immersed in English novels and occasionally tried his hand at writing. Years later, that love for literature would find its way into the name of his second daughter.“Sahithi is similar to Sahitya, which means literature,” Lokesh explained. But the name had another influence, one rooted in music.Lokesh comes from a family with a rich artistic background. His father’s side of the family was involved in theatre, and music was also part of their household. Lokesh himself was a keen singer, winning several prizes at the state level. Among the ragas he particularly admired was Amruthavarshini, whose name he wanted to draw upon for his daughter.His wife, however, felt that literature deserved a place in the name, too. And so, the two influences came together — Sahithi, inspired by literature, and Varshini, drawn from music.“But eventually, she didn’t belong to either of the two and chose the 64 squares,” Lokesh said with a smile. “She made a name for herself in a different domain.”Lokesh was born in a remote village on the edge of Yarada Hills, close enough to the sea that you could see it from the top. But there was no electricity. Before his father secured a job, the family had depended on fishing for a livelihood, as generations on his father’s side had done in a village near Srikakulam district. Walking to the next colony for food took half an hour.He still became a school topper and then a state-ranked student in the engineering entrance. But the family could not afford it. Lokesh's father had retired, and there was no financial backup. He left the course, took a small job after completing a diploma course, and finished an engineering degree by correspondence. Years later, he joined HPCL as an officer.Lokesh was in his early 30s when he started taking chess seriously. He ran a literature club, a small group that exchanged idioms, short stories, and poems by email, trying to sharpen their English in Vizag.One member, Dinesh, a young medical student who lived opposite him, brought a huge chess trophy to the club one day after becoming the Andhra University chess champion. Having learnt that Lokesh had played chess as a child, Dinesh turned up at his house at ten one night with a chessboard.Lokesh's wife Jaya Sri, however, was left unimpressed, asking the two of them to play the game on the balcony.Lokesh was close to winning the first game and then collapsed. The next day Dinesh won two more. The day after, he won two again, and told Lokesh he had found his weakness. "I took it as a challenge," Lokesh recalled. "I wanted to win one game against him. That is how it started."He bought a book from a local shop and began reading in the refinery's control room, where officers sit around digital boards operating the plant. He would sketch positions on paper, then rub them out and redraw. A senior colleague, VS Prasad, caught him doing it and asked if he played chess. Lokesh begged him not to tell the bosses. Prasad took him home instead, to a shelf of 40 or 50 chess books.One was Max Euwe's The Road to Chess Mastery. For a man in love with literature, it certainly felt like a heaven. "It was like a Sherlock Holmes novel kind of a thing," he told this website.Soon, beating Dinesh became a routine. "I won some five to ten games straight away," he shared.Within three months, he made the HPCL team, and within six months of that he was at the national selections for the Petroleum Sports Promotion Board (PSPB), finishing second. He played for the board for roughly seven years, often captaining HPCL.At tournaments, he shared the hall with grandmasters such as Pentala Harikrishna, Shyam Sundar and Koneru Humpy, among others.He was never the strongest player in those rooms. Nevertheless, what he had was an appetite for classical chess. He would take an opening idea from a book, set up the position, and put it to the GMs. They told him he would one day be one of the finest coaches in the country."So that was the foundation," he said, giving us a touch of the philosophy behind Sahithi's approach today.The formal coach within Lokesh became active when her daughters started playing. Despite Sahithi showing early promise, he never set himself a target of IM or GM. What he wanted was a particular kind of game."I always had a very big dream to make her someone like Fischer and Kasparov, not a GM and all," he noted. "I never thought of making IM, GM and then celebrate it. Those moments are important, definitely, in life to cherish and move forward. But my dream was to make her someone like a legend."That ambition shows in how she plays. She goes for sacrifices and attacking positions, and her games grabbed early attention.At 14, she was rated over 2200. Her attacking play drew praise from Scottish Grandmaster, world-famous chess trainer, and author Jacob Aagaard. She also beat women's world champion Mariya Muzychuk."She never fears the opponent. She just plays her style," her coach said.Soon, she had also won a stack of age-group medals, among them Asian and Commonwealth golds.Then came COVID. Sahithi was at her peak, rated highly and seeded at the top of her age groups, and the tournaments stopped. She missed almost three years of competitive chess."You are playing so well, and suddenly, you don't have the option of playing continuously," Lokesh said. "That was really annoying."Leave from work was a problem even before the pandemic. She qualified for a world youth championship (the Cadets tournament) but could not travel. After the lockdowns, Lokesh took long leave and moved the family abroad, reasoning that a rented apartment would cost less than repeated flights. It was a gamble, and he knew it.It also exposed a different problem. Online chess meant every game she played in open tournaments was published, and opponents could prepare against her at the click of a button. A player who loved to surprise people was suddenly easy to study. She tried switching openings from one day to the next, which backfired against stronger opposition.Playing 2300-rated players, he explained, you cannot get away with half-prepared systems. "It did backfire for almost a year," he said.But she came out of it understanding more openings than before. And in 2022 she played at the Chess Olympiad in Chennai, a member of India's C women's team and among the youngest in the squad. "Playing for India is always a special thing," Lokesh told this website.After the Olympiad, the targets slipped away. Sahithi secured a 13th-place finish at the FIDE Women's World Rapid Chess Championship 2023 held in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, which also earned praise from former five-time world champion Viswanathan Anand. She was close to 2300 but not there, and the company could not keep granting leave.The trips abroad were expensive. HPCL contributed around Rs 10 lakh to Sahithi's career, and the Andhra Pradesh government gave a similar amount, but it was not enough."I had to sell an apartment," Lokesh revealed. His wife's gold was pledged. He was running out of options when he reached the most difficult decision almost three years back. "There was only one way. I had to quit my job," he recalled.He resigned and set up a chess academy, which he admits was harder than it sounded. A start in Hyderabad did not work for about ten months, partly because he was away at tournaments with Sahithi.Then, following a heart attack, he had a bypass operation, the heart surgery that forced him to stop for months and reduced both his income and his strength.Around the same time, relatives pressed him to make Sahithi finish class 10. She took nine months away from chess to do it."It sets the morale down," he said of the surgery. "Financially, it also consumes."Jaya Sri was a rock throughout. "I appreciate my wife more than me to be more braver than myself," he said. For a woman who was not earning and had no connection to chess, living with selling property, shifting country, and watching her husband leave his job, he considers it a far harder act of faith than his own.His elder daughter Falguni, now a FIDE arbiter, helped too, paying her own fees and rent by teaching classes.The decision to open the chess academy turned out better than he feared. Back in Visakhapatnam, the academy grew.His student Ajay santhosh Parvathareddy has amassed two GM norms and is now on the verge of beocoming a grand master. Aarav Sinha has collected four IM norms, and others gained hundreds of rating points within months on the European circuit. More than fifteen players now train with him, and he is writing a book on the 2200 level."After surgery, I have had bigger achievements compared to pre-surgery," he remarked.Sahithi was his first student. She remains the one he measures the rest against. But she is not, by his father's account, in the best place mentally."She is a little demotivated, to be frank," Lokesh added. The three lost years still weigh on her. Her advice, however, is the same every time."How you start is not as important as how you end," he tells her. "Whatever you missed in those years, no regrets for that. Just look at what opportunities you have."The plan is to build strength rather than chase a rating. "If you are 2500, you should be able to play like a 2500," he explained. "It should not merely happen with your rating. You should deserve it."The harder obstacle is access. Official events such as the Asian Championships, Commonwealth events and World Juniors come with hotel costs that the family cannot easily meet. Lokesh believes that if Sahithi is given those platforms, results and sponsors will follow. If not, he will keep creating his own opportunities."I'm optimistic that way, rather than regretting not having big sponsors," he acknowledged, thanking Pravaha Foundation for currently sponsoring the chess prodigy in her journey."There are no big names in this journey. No godfathers. You don't require big names to make your stamp. It is your willpower, your passion for the game, your determination, and how you sustain in the difficult phases that take you forward."Perhaps Sagar Shah had got it right all those years ago. Like rice that takes time to cook to perfection over a gentle flame, Sahithi Varshini, too, may need time to come into her own. And when she does, it may well be to carry forward the legacy of those who came before her in chess, sooner rather than later.
Article Summary: Vizag-born prodigy Sahithi Varshini recently became India’s latest Woman Grandmaster (WGM) Her father Lokeswara Moogi Rao, her only coach to date, tells TimesofIndia.com: "This is just a mere beginning"

Article Title: Coach axed after explosive selection row! India name 166 athletes for Asian Para Games 2026
Article Text:
Para-badminton player Pramod Bhagat, para-archer Rakesh Kumar, para table tennis player Bhavina Patel, and others during the send-off ceremony. (PTI Photo)

Controversial shooting selection; cyclists' protest fails to change squad

Sheetal Devi, Bhavina Patel among India's medal hopes

NEW DELHI: The Sports Ministry has dropped under-fire para-shooting coach Jai Prakash Nautiyal from India's contingent for the Asian Para Games 2026, approving a 166-athlete squad for the continental event in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, amid a controversy-marred selection process that triggered protests by shooters and cyclists.The Games are scheduled to begin on October 18, with India set to compete across 10 disciplines. Long-serving national coach Jeevan L Rai has replaced Nautiyal in the squad following allegations of irregularities in the selection process.As per a PTI report, Nautiyal had faced allegations of not following established selection criteria and demanding kickbacks in exchange for selecting shooters. Several athletes protested outside the Sports Authority of India (SAI) headquarters, demanding his removal and an investigation into the charges.The aggrieved shooters also met Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya to present their grievances after attempting to disrupt the contingent's send-off ceremony last week.With 166 athletes approved, India will have a total contingent of 275, including 94 team officials and support staff and 15 contingent staff members.The 13-member shooting squad, which has been at the centre of the controversy, features Paralympic gold medallist Avani Lekhara and Mona Agarwal, among others.Agarwal recently secured a silver medal at the World Championships in Korea, earning India a quota place for the 2028 Los Angeles Paralympics.The Ministry has also resisted pressure for last-minute additions to the cycling squad despite protests by omitted athletes. Only Paralympian Arshad Shaik was approved from among those in contention, having comfortably met the selection criteria.Six other cyclists had been selected by the Cycling Federation of India and the Paralympic Committee of India (PCI), but were subsequently left out for failing to satisfy the prescribed criteria.The decision comes amid questions over the selection process, with athletes seeking greater transparency in the composition of the Indian contingent.Para-athletics forms the biggest part of India's contingent, with 62 athletes, including 46 men, and a support staff of 36. World Championships medallist Simran, a visually impaired sprinter, is also part of the squad. After her previous guide, Umar Saifi, was caught in a doping case, she will compete with a new guide, Shivam.India's other medal prospects include Paralympic silver medallist Bhavina Patel in table tennis and a strong badminton contingent of 28 players, comprising 17 men and 11 women.Former world No. 1 and Tokyo Paralympic gold medallist Pramod Bhagat and former Paralympic silver medallist Suhas Yathiraj headline the badminton squad, which has been allocated 11 support staff members.In archery, 19-year-old Sheetal Devi, a double gold medallist at the previous Para Asian Games, will be among India's leading contenders. The world champion will be joined by 18-year-old Payal Nag, who grabbed attention by defeating Sheetal at the World Archery Para Series in Bangkok earlier this year.With a sizeable contingent and several established champions in its ranks, India will look to make a strong impression in Japan, even as the selection controversy casts a shadow over the team's preparations.
Article Summary: The Sports Ministry has dropped under-fire para-shooting coach Jai Prakash Nautiyal from India's contingent for the Asian Para Games 2026. The decision comes amid questions over the selection process. India will have a total contingent of 275, including 94 team officials and support staff and 15 contingent staff members.

Article Title: Sarah Dambanevana, first Zimbabwean female umpire in Women's T20 World Cup, passes away at 36
Article Text:
Sarah Dambanevana

From player to a trailblazing umpire

Zimbabwe Cricket pays tribute

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Former Zimbabwe fast bowler and international umpire Sarah Dambanevana has died in Harare at the age of 36. She passed away on Monday, October 12, after spending months in hospital following a medical procedure in March, Zimbabwe Cricket confirmed.Dambanevana represented Zimbabwe as a player between 2009 and 2014 before moving into umpiring, where she went on to make history on the international stage.Dambanevana began her senior international umpiring career in September 2023. Earlier that year, she became the first Zimbabwean woman to officiate in a World Cup final when she stood in the final of the Under-19 Women's T20 World Cup between India and England in South Africa.She later officiated at the Women's T20 World Cup in the UAE in 2024, becoming first Zimbabwean female umpire to do so.She also took field in the Women's ODI World Cup in India and Sri Lanka in 2025. At the latter tournament, she was part of the first all-female panel of match officials.In total, she officiated in 63 senior international matches, including 42 women's T20 Internationals, 11 women's ODIs and 10 men's T20 Internationals.She also worked in domestic cricket and international youth tournaments. Before becoming an umpire, she played for Zimbabwe, including at the 2011 World Cup Qualifier. She joined the ICC's development panel of umpires in 2022.Zimbabwe Cricket chairman Tavengwa Mukuhlani praised Dambanevana for her contribution to the game as both a player and an umpire."Sarah served Zimbabwe with distinction, first as a player and then as an umpire whose ability earned her a place on the world stage," Mukuhlani said. "Watching her stand in a World Cup final was a moment of immense pride for our cricket community and our country. She showed young Zimbabwean women that they belong at the highest levels of the game, including in roles where opportunities had long been limited."Through her achievements, she opened doors and gave others the confidence to pursue their own ambitions. We will remember her dedication, her professionalism and her willingness to help others grow. Her passing leaves a painful void in our cricket family, but the example she set will continue to inspire those who follow in her footsteps."
Article Summary: Sarah Dambanevana has died in Harare at the age of 36. She was the first Zimbabwean woman to officiate in a World Cup final. Before becoming an umpire, she played for Zimbabwe. Zimbabwe Cricket chairman Tavengwa Mukuhlani praised her contribution.

India's own project

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) has confirmed seven interested parties for the 2036 Summer Olympics: India, Germany, Qatar, South Korea, South Africa, Türkiye and Hungary. With the process currently at the dialogue stage, the bids will be shortlisted in March 2027, preferred hosts will be identified in December 2028, and the host will be announced in mid-2029.Germany's candidate is Munich; South Korea's project is associated with Jeonju and Jeonbuk, as well as Seoul; Qatar's is centred on Doha; and South Africa is considering a multi-city or nationwide model. Hungary has designated Budapest as its central venue, while Türkiye is planning to host the 2036 Summer Olympics in Istanbul and India in Ahmedabad.South Korea is no stranger to hosting the Olympics. Seoul hosted the 1988 Summer Olympics, a landmark event in the country's emergence on the international stage. PyeongChang hosted the 2018 Winter Olympics, giving the country experience of hosting both the Summer and Winter Games.The domestic selection process produced a significant change in direction. The Korean Sport & Olympic Committee selected Jeonbuk (North Jeolla Province), with Jeonju as its focal city, as the country's domestic candidate.The wider discussion has also involved Seoul, which has its own infrastructure and Olympic legacy.Jeonbuk has been pushing an Olympic plan that uses venues across the province and other Korean cities, while Seoul's supporters have argued that its existing facilities and transport infrastructure make it a more credible option.The regional approach could distribute the benefits of the Games beyond the capital. It also raises a practical question: how will the country present a single, coherent proposal to the IOC when different domestic stakeholders have championed different hosting models?South Korea's advantage is its proven experience in delivering the Olympics. Ahmedabad, by contrast, is building its case around the 2030 Commonwealth Games and the possibility of using the Olympics to transform India's sporting ecosystem.The comparison, therefore, is not simply about how many stadiums each city has. It is about whether Ahmedabad can offer the IOC an equally convincing account of how the venues will work, how athletes will move between them, and what will remain after the Games.Qatar is selling accumulated investment and operational readiness. Rather than making the Olympics the starting point for a major infrastructure build-out, it wants to demonstrate that much of the necessary infrastructure is already in place.Doha previously sought to host the Summer Olympics in 2016 and 2020 but failed to reach the final stage of either selection process. The 2016 project was rejected at the applicant stage, while the 2020 campaign did not make the final group of candidate cities.Since then, Qatar has substantially expanded its major-event credentials. Its record includes:- The 2022 FIFA World Cup.- The 2023 AFC Asian Cup.- The 2024 World Aquatics Championships.- The 2030 Asian Games, which Qatar is scheduled to host.This record gives Qatar something that a first-time Olympic host cannot easily replicate: experience in managing a major-event ecosystem, including stadiums, accommodation, transport, broadcasting and international sporting operations.Qatar's pitch is centred on Doha and the wider metropolitan area, with Lusail and Al Rayyan among the locations relevant to its existing sports infrastructure.The Qatar Olympic Committee has said that approximately 95% of the required sports infrastructure is already available. The final project will still need to establish the suitability of venues, their capacity, operating arrangements and any gaps that must be addressed.Its approach is tied to Qatar National Vision 2030, with an emphasis on sustainability, inclusion, legacy and limiting unnecessary construction. The country is also looking to build on the facilities and experience developed for the 2022 World Cup.One important complication is the calendar. Doha's summer temperatures could make a conventional July-August Olympics difficult. Qatar's 2022 World Cup was moved to November and December because of the heat, and a Summer Olympics in Qatar would face a comparable question about competition conditions and scheduling.Qatar sets the benchmark for infrastructure readiness and delivery experience. Its challenge is not whether it can build major sports facilities, but whether it can make the case for a Summer Olympics that meets athletes' needs, accounts for the climate and delivers an enduring public legacy.Ahmedabad can counter with a different argument: hosting would accelerate the development of a sports ecosystem in a country with a vast population and a large potential athlete base. However, the Indian proposal will need to be precise about which facilities already exist, which are planned and how each investment will be used after 2036.Qatar's experience also offers a warning for India: successfully delivering one mega-event does not, by itself, settle questions about long-term legacy, sustainability or international scrutiny.Munich, which hosted the 1972 Games, wants to show that a modern Olympics need not be a giant construction project. Its proposition centres on existing venues, short distances, a familiar Olympic setting and the conversion of Games infrastructure into long-term public assets.The year 2036 has particular significance: it would fall exactly 100 years after the Berlin Games, which the Nazi regime exploited for propaganda. This gives Germany an opportunity to frame the event around democratic values and a very different modern identity, but it also makes the anniversary politically sensitive.Germany's domestic selection process was competitive. Munich defeated Cologne-Rhine-Ruhr in the German Olympic Sports Confederation's selection, winning by 90 votes to 51. Hamburg's earlier plans had been rejected in a referendum, while Berlin withdrew its proposal. Munich was eventually selected as Germany's candidate for the 2036, 2040 or 2044 Games.The German Olympic Sports Confederation's official concept, Munich for Germany, has several distinguishing features:- Existing facilities: The Olympic Park, which hosted events in 1972, is the centrepiece.- Short distances: Munich wants to keep a large proportion of competition venues within a compact geographical area.- A recognisable city setting: Locations such as the English Garden, Nymphenburg Palace and Odeonsplatz feature in the wider vision.- Post-Games housing: The Olympic and Paralympic Village is intended to become a climate-neutral, accessible neighbourhood for more than 10,000 people.- Sustainability: The bid promotes the circular use of resources and a legacy that extends beyond the event itself.The DOSB says approximately half of all competitions would take place in the Olympic Park. The concept is intended to reduce the need for new construction and make use of Munich's existing sporting infrastructure.Munich's domestic public mandate is also notable: 66.4% of residents voted in favour of hosting the Olympic and Paralympic Games in a referendum.Munich's strongest argument is that it may not need to build as much as its rivals. That is a direct challenge to Ahmedabad's model. India's plans involve a major programme of urban development and sports infrastructure around the city. Munich, by contrast, is presenting existing venues and legacy reuse as competitive advantages.For Ahmedabad, the lesson is to explain not just how much infrastructure will be developed, but also how much can be reused, how much it will cost to maintain and what the city will gain in return. A compelling Olympic proposal must be an urban development plan as well as a sports master plan.South Africa wants to bring the Summer Olympics to Africa for the first time. Its case combines the symbolic significance of being the first African host with the country's existing experience of delivering major international sporting events.South Africa has never hosted an Olympic Games. Its major-event record includes the 1995 Rugby World Cup and the 2010 FIFA World Cup.The latter is especially relevant because it demonstrated the country's ability to stage a global event across multiple venues and cities. It also offers an example of how a major tournament can be used to develop or upgrade infrastructure.The country has explored hosting the Olympics for several years, with the government approving its entry into the IOC's Continuous Dialogue process for a potential 2036 or 2040 Games.The proposal initially outlined by South African Olympic leadership is a multi-city model involving Cape Town, Johannesburg and Durban.The logic is to distribute venues and responsibilities across existing urban centres rather than force the entire event into one city. It draws inspiration from the use of multiple locations at Paris 2024 and aims to make greater use of existing facilities.The three cities offer different strengths:- Cape Town: A globally recognisable setting and a proposed centre of the national project.- Johannesburg: Major-event experience and established sporting infrastructure, including FNB Stadium.- Durban: Existing major sports facilities, including Moses Mabhida Stadium.The final configuration remains subject to development. South African officials have also indicated that a preferred host city would need to be selected as the project progresses.South Africa and India are both trying to make a larger historical argument through the Olympics. For South Africa, success would mean hosting the first Summer Olympics on African soil. For India, it would mean hosting the country's first Olympic Games and taking a major step towards its ambition of becoming a global sporting power.Both can argue that hosting would expand participation and create a wider sporting legacy. Both also need to show that their national ambitions are backed by credible funding, reliable governance and realistic plans for coordinating the host locations.The key distinction is that South Africa's project is explicitly designed to spread the Games across multiple cities. India's proposal is centred on Ahmedabad, even though the benefits of hosting would be national.Istanbul is trying to turn repeated Olympic disappointment into a stronger, more mature proposal, using existing infrastructure and upcoming international events to demonstrate readiness. Istanbul has made five previous unsuccessful attempts to host the Summer Olympics: 2000, 2004, 2008, 2012 and 2020.The 2020 campaign is especially relevant because Istanbul reached the final vote, finishing behind Tokyo. The city therefore has experience of an Olympic campaign at the highest level but has yet to convince the IOC to award it the Games.Türkiye's current bid process has been underway for several years. The Turkish National Olympic Committee (TMOK) says it formally backed Istanbul's candidacy in April 2024 and entered the IOC's Continuous Dialogue process.Istanbul's proposal combines existing venues and infrastructure with a wider national effort to demonstrate its ability to organise major competitions.The city's Olympic authorities, the Ministry of Youth and Sports, Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality and the Turkish Paralympic Committee have been involved in presenting the project's vision to the IOC. Their work has addressed the expected impact of the Games, the legacy plan and the relationship between the Olympic project and Istanbul's urban development objectives.The most important practical milestone is the 2027 European Games, which Türkiye intends to use as a rehearsal for its Olympic ambition.TMOK has described the event as a live rehearsal and a test of confidence. The intention is to demonstrate venue readiness, transport and logistics, operational capacity and the ability to work with international sporting bodies before the IOC makes its decision on the 2036 Games.Türkiye's government has also pointed to its experience of hosting major sporting competitions, ongoing investment in swimming facilities and the availability of an Olympic Village. Those claims will need to be assessed alongside the complete competition-venue plan and the wider logistics of the proposed Games.Istanbul's advantage is that it has repeatedly pursued the Olympics and understands the demands of the bidding process. However, its history also demonstrates that persistence and a strong city identity do not guarantee success.The 2027 European Games offer a useful parallel with Ahmedabad's role in the 2030 Commonwealth Games. Both cities have a major multisport event that can serve as evidence of their ability to host something larger.For Ahmedabad, the critical question will be whether the Commonwealth Games become a genuine test of operational readiness and long-term planning, rather than simply a milestone on the way to an Olympic bid.Hungary is exploring a bid to host the 2036 Olympic and Paralympic Games in Budapest, with a vision centred on existing and temporary venues rather than the construction of new permanent stadiums. The proposed model envisages at least 80% of events taking place in Hungary, with the possibility of sharing venues with neighbouring countries.Budapest has pursued Olympic hosting ambitions for the 1916, 1920, 1936 and 1960 Games, but none resulted in the city being awarded the event. Its most recent campaign was for the 2024 Olympics, but it was withdrawn in February 2017 after the Momentum Movement gathered approximately 266,000 signatures demanding a referendum on the proposal.Since then, Hungary has hosted several major international sporting events, including the 2017 and 2022 World Aquatics Championships and the 2023 World Athletics Championships. These events have strengthened the country's experience in organising international competitions, although an Olympic bid would still require broad political consensus and firm financial guarantees.The proposed Games would draw on Hungary's existing sporting infrastructure, including Puskás Aréna, the National Athletics Centre, MVM Dome and Duna Aréna. Where suitable facilities are unavailable, organisers could consider temporary venues or explore sharing facilities with other countries. Preliminary discussions have included possible venues in Vienna, Bratislava, Košice, Brno, Ljubljana, Zagreb, Belgrade and Cluj-Napoca, although no final agreements have been reached.Hungary's proposition is about hosting the Olympics with less new permanent construction, while Ahmedabad's is about using the Olympics to accelerate sporting and urban development.- Venues: Hungary prioritises existing and temporary facilities, potentially supplemented by venues across Central Europe. Ahmedabad's plans centre on a proposed sports enclave and wider infrastructure development.- Legacy: Hungary emphasises avoiding underused stadiums and investing in infrastructure that Budapest already needs. Ahmedabad frames the Games as a catalyst for wider participation and India's sporting ambitions.- Experience: Hungary has recently staged major international championships. Ahmedabad's 2030 Commonwealth Games offer an opportunity to demonstrate its ability to deliver a multisport event.- Main obstacle: Hungary needs political agreement and a workable cross-border model. Ahmedabad needs to demonstrate that its infrastructure plans, funding, governance and operational capabilities can meet Olympic requirements.- The key contrast: Hungary asks whether the Olympics can be staged with minimal new permanent stadium construction. Ahmedabad asks whether the Olympics can justify and accelerate a major programme of development.India's campaign is framed around the vision "Rising Together" and the idea that hosting the Games could transform the country's sporting ecosystem, rather than merely stage a fortnight of competition. The Indian Olympic Association (IOA) has described the ambition as an opportunity to increase participation, strengthen communities and create opportunities through sport.IOA CEO Raghuram Iyer has also made the ambition explicit: India wants to become a sporting superpower, with the longer-term goal of entering the world's top five or top 10 sporting nations.- Sports City: Plans associated with the Commonwealth Games include 11 sports complexes and complementary facilities such as gyms, swimming pools and training spaces.- Municipal investment: Ahmedabad's draft municipal budget for 2026-27 earmarked ₹17,018 crore for development, including mobility, sustainability and urban development.- 2030 Commonwealth Games: These provide a nearer-term opportunity to test venue delivery and event operations.- 2038 Asian Games: India has also pursued Ahmedabad as a possible host, potentially creating a sequence of major multisport events leading towards the Olympic ambition.
Article Summary: The International Olympic Committee (IOC) has confirmed seven interested parties for the 2036 Summer Olympics. India, Germany, Qatar, South Korea, South Africa, Türkiye and Hungary are bidding. The bids will be shortlisted in March 2027, preferred hosts will be identified in December 2028, and the host will be announced in mid-2029.

Article Title: ‘DGC game of chess tougher this year’: Shiv Kapur decodes the lies and breaks at Delhi’s iconic golf course

Shiv Kapur (ANI Photo)

Tougher after the Gary Player redesign: After the Gary Player redesign of the Lodhi course, it’s a bit more strategic. Earlier, the greens were fairly flat, so you got a lot of birdie opportunities. The main changes were the bunkering and the contouring of the greens. The greens have a lot more slope, more pin positions. There are certain pins this week that you won’t be able to go at. NEW DELHI: Rory McIlroy, superstar draw of the DP World India Championship for the second year running, would probably like a deeper reading of the jungle book that is the Delhi Golf Club this time round. Perhaps, deep is not the right word here with the bogeyman in the bushes listening.“The next time I hit my driver will be in Abu Dhabi,” the World No. 2 had said after his Pro-Am rehearsal here last year at the inaugural DPWIC. Laughter had ensued on a lazy Wednesday afternoon. And the Masters champ eventually finished T-26th at 11-under before packing his bags on Sunday, with a little regret and a few lessons. But the best thing about golf is that you immediately move on.Two strokes behind Rory was Shiv Kapur that week, as the bestplaced Indian. Kapur has moved on too, from his childhood backyard. The Asian Tour website tells us that once he had great fun shooting a 44-over 166 at an AsiaPacific Juniors event, and for the 44-year-old, the many meanderings on the course over the years had yielded laughter, pain, pressure, and finally an Asian Tour triumph at the Panasonic India in 2017.“Monkey is finally off my back now,” he had said, smiling out of relief then. It was probably the same emotions experienced by McIlroy at Augusta in 2025.Based out of Dubai now, Shiv returns to India to play IGPL events, and work on course projects — the 9-hole golf course in Lonavala opens Nov 22, where every Wednesday, children and people from the local community will be exempt from fees. But the minute he takes the gateway to the green haven amidst the bustle of central Delhi, there is no better place to be.“Somebody of Rory’s or Tommy Fleetwood’s calibre may not struggle but certainly, it’s a very unique week on the Tour because they don’t play too many courses like this. It’s like a game of chess where you have to place it in certain areas,” Shiv talked about why strategy is valued over brute force here. “It is more of a power game these days where people outmuscle courses. But DGC is one of those classic tests where you have to think your way around.It’s a week where most players will probably not have the big stick in the bag.”He doesn’t see a repeat of Fleetwood’s winning score of 22-under. “The rough is around 4 to 5 inches, which is, at par with the US Open. You have to keep it in the short grass. It’s going to be a tougher test.”

On the 18th, the front section of the green is very, very narrow, so you have about a five-yard entrance to enter. The real challenge comes when you stand on the 14th tee.

Article Title: ISSF World Cup: Rhythm Sangwan misses bronze, Indian rifle men fail to enter final
Article Text:
Rhythm Sangwan (NRAI Photo)

PUNE: It was a no-podium day for Indians at the ISSF World Cup in Cairo as both, pistol and rifle shooters failed to show their best on Monday.Barring Rhythm Sangwan, who finished fourth in women’s 25m sports pistol final, other five Indians couldn’t even enter the finals of their respective categories.Rhythm, the Paris Games participant, missed the bronze by two hits in the final that was won by Singapore’s Xiu Yi Teh. The silver and bronze were won by France's Heloise Fourre and Bulgaria's Miroslava Mincheva, respectively. Rhythm, 22, scored 26 in the final and was in medal contention till the seventh series.She looked good to seal the bronze, at least, but in the eighth series, the Haryana shooter missed four out of five shots, while Miroslava, who was a point behind Rhythm, went two points ahead to push the Indian for elimination.Earlier, Rhythm qualified for the final on top, by scoring 587 in the qualifier. In 2023, the Indian had broken the 29-year-old record in the event by scoring 595 at the World Cup in Baku. The previous record was held by Bulgarian shooter Diana Iorgova, who had shot 594 in Milan World Cup in May 1994. However, the Indian went out of form after a dismal show in the Paris Olympics.“It was a good match. I am happy about the way I shot in the qualification round and then in the final.I just had one bad series and that happened to be the last one. Unfortunately, I couldn’t win the medal, but I am satisfied with the way I shot,” Rhythm, who has played in only two international tournaments since Paris, told TOI.“I think such days give you confidence for the future,” she added.Other Indians in fray, Divya TS (582) and Chinki Yadav (580), finished 10th and 16th, respectively.In the men’s 10m air rifle event, Paris Games fourth-place finisher, Arjun Babuta failed to enter the final after finishing 16th with a score of 630. Other Indians, Dhanush Srikanth (629.4) and Paarth Makhija (629.3) were placed 21st and 22nd, respectively.
Article Summary: Rhythm Sangwan missed the bronze by two hits in the final that was won by Singapore’s Xiu Yi Teh. Paris Games fourth-place finisher, Arjun Babuta failed to enter the final after finishing 16th with a score of 630.

Article Title: Asian Para Games: Coach row, court battles, clearance delays deepen chaos
Article Text:
File Pic: Shooter Manish Narwal

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: With less than a week to go before the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Para Games starts, India’s preparations have been clouded by selection disputes, coaching omissions and administrative delays, leaving athletes in para shooting, cycling, badminton, table tennis and boccia grappling with uncertainty.On Monday, nine of India’s 13 selected para shooters met Sports Authority of India (SAI) officials and the sport’s project officer at SAI headquarters here, expressing dissatisfaction over the omission of chief coach J P Nautiyal from the contingent. Armourer and assistant coach Shivam Tyagi has also been left out.The aggrieved shooters urged authorities to reconsider the decision, with some expressing apprehension about competing without Nautiyal. Among those raising concerns were Manish Narwal, Mona Agarwal, Nihal Singh, Shrishti Arora, Swaroop Mahavir Unhalkar, Rakesh Nidagundi, Sumedha Pathak and Bhakti Sharma, who have won major international medals under his guidance.Bhakti, a deaf and non-speaking shooter who relies on specialised communication, reportedly broke down during the meeting, while Sumedha expressed doubts about competing without her coach.Pistol coach Rakesh Singh and support staff member Pavittar accompanied the shooters.The dispute comes as the ministry finally cleared the pending disciplines late on Monday evening, according to sources. The ministry’s push came as para badminton and table tennis contingents were scheduled to leave for Japan on Tuesday evening and there was considerable delay in announcing their final sanctions. With these approvals, the Indian contingent has been cleared across disciplines, barring pending court cases, including that of para cycling.The Oct 10 partial sanction covered eight disciplines and listed 128 athletes — 90 male and 38 female — alongside 91 officials, taking the contingent to 219 members. Badminton, table tennis and boccia were excluded at that stage.The delay also affected kit distribution. Athletes visiting the Paralympic Committee of India (PCI) office on Monday afternoon to collect ceremonial and competition kits returned empty-handed as approvals were awaited. Pramod Bhagat, India’s opening-ceremony flag-bearer, had worn fellow shuttler Sukant Kadam’s ceremonial outfit at the October 8 send-off because his own did not fit.Last-minute clearances have left athletes with little time to correct ill-fitting kits, organise equipment, and prepare for departure. In table tennis, competition begins on Oct 16, following classification checks on Oct 15. Wheelchair players need time to acclimatise and adjust their equipment, while paddlers will have just a day to rest after reaching Nagoya before classification begins.Despite the final approvals, five badminton names — Chirag Baretha, Manisha Patel, Shashank Kumar, Ammu Beulah Mohan and Rachna Patel — have not been sanctioned, sources said. LY Suhas has been cleared. Kalpesh Thakkar, secretary of the Table Tennis Association of Baroda, has also not been cleared.In para cycling, five qualified athletes have challenged their exclusion in the Delhi High Court under Articles 14 and 21, questioning the decision to retain only one cyclist despite six recommendations. The case will be heard again on Tuesday, with an interim decision expected.
Article Summary: Nine of India’s 13 selected para shooters met Sports Authority of India (SAI) officials. They expressed dissatisfaction over the omission of chief coach J P Nautiyal. The aggrieved shooters urged authorities to reconsider the decision. The dispute comes as the ministry finally cleared the pending disciplines late on Monday.

Article Title: Jithin’s stoppage-time strike helps NEUFC sink Mohun Bagan
Article Text:
Jithin MS after scoring in Guwahati on Monday. (Pic credit: NEUFC)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

They could not overcome the heavyweights in pre-season, losing in the semifinals of the Durand Cup and settling for a draw in the IFA Shield group stage.However, Juan Pedro Benali's men delivered when it mattered most as NorthEast United FC snatched a dramatic late 1-0 win against Mohun Bagan Super Giant in their Indian Super League opener in Guwahati on Monday.Playing in front of their fans at the Indira Gandhi Athletic Stadium, it was super-sub Jithin MS who struck the winner in the first minute of stoppage time after Bagan had dominated much of the 90 minutes with their attacks, while NEUFC relied on the brilliance of Alaaeddine Ajaraie to breach the visitors' defence.The first half produced some enthralling end-to-end action, with Mohun Bagan pressing from the word go and the Highlanders responding with attacks of their own after the opening 10 minutes.It was Lallianzuala Chhangte, in his new green-and-maroon colours, who dominated the early exchanges, having been named in the starting XI by coach Panagiotis Dilmperis ahead of regular Bagan winger Manvir Singh. Soon after, however, fellow new signing Lee Erwin began to grow into the game.The Scot also came closest to breaking the deadlock with a volley that dropped into the goal after hitting the bar, only for the offside flag to deny him.His physicality and pace began to pose all sorts of problems for the NEUFC defence. However, the Highlanders' new signing Nikhil Barla remained up to the task in his defensive role.The combination of Chhangte and Erwin made a Bagan breakthrough look imminent, only for the NEUFC defence, led by skipper Asheer Akhtar, to soak up the pressure every time.At the other end, Highlanders talisman Ajaraie looked threatening with his individual brilliance, while Ethyan Gonzalez's crosses repeatedly found runners inside the box, but each move was thwarted by the blocking and marking of Alberto Rodriguez and Lalengmawia Ralte.It was Rodriguez who came close for the visitors in the 43rd minute when his long-range effort whistled past the top-left corner of the NEUFC goal.While both coaches made a couple of changes after the break, it was the combination of Sahal Abdul Samad and Erwin that created two chances in quick succession in the 54th minute. Erwin first produced a feeble effort from close range after a Sahal pass and then failed to keep down a tricky volley, sending it over the bar.Soon after, Dilmperis replaced Erwin with Miguel Ferreira and brought on regular attackers Liston Colaco and Manvir Singh, along with Kashmiri forward Suhail Ahmed Bhat, in search of the elusive goal.Ajaraie had a couple of good chances in the 72nd and 75th minutes respectively but had Mehtab Singh stand strong with a tackle in the first while his dipping long volley that beat goalkeeper was disallowed by the referee’s whistle.On the other end, an incessant series of attacks from Bagan was met with some frantic but successful defending from the home side as Benali’s men mostly resorted to counter-attacks to find a goal against the run of play.Bhat could have got Bagan a goal towards the end when he failed to connect to a perfect cross from Colaco from the right at goal-mouth in the 87th minute and hit the woodwork a couple of minutes later.However, roared on by their fans, NEUFC began creating chances of their own towards the end of regulation time and, in the 95th minute, the ball fell to Jithin after a Gonzalez piledriver struck the woodwork. The dependable midfielder made no mistake, calmly turning the rebound into the winner.
Article Summary: NorthEast United FC snatch a dramatic late 1-0 win against Mohun Bagan Super Giant in their Indian Super League opener in Guwahati on Monday. Super-sub Jithin MS struck the winner in the first minute of stoppage time after Bagan had dominated much of the 90 minutes.

Article Title: From introduction to skeet gun at 13 to Asian Games bronze: Parinaz Dhaliwal’s journey of precision, perseverance and the right support
Article Text:
Parinaaz Dhaliwal

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: For Parinaaz Dhaliwal, success in skeet shooting is about much more than hitting targets. It is a combination of technical precision, mental strength, financial backing and the ability to find balance under pressure. After years of investing in her game, the Asian Games medallist believes experience, the right coaching environment and an unwavering support system have helped her take significant strides forward.When Parinaaz looks back at her journey in shooting, she does not attribute her progress to one competition, one coach or one breakthrough moment. Instead, she sees it as an evolution shaped by years of training, international exposure and lessons learnt along the way. The bronze medal in the women’s skeet team event at the Asian Games 2026 at Aichi-Nagoya in Japan alongside Raiza Dhillon and Maheshwari Chauhan, was a significant milestone in that journey.“It was bits of everything, to be honest,” she says, reflecting on the difference between her previous Asian Games appearance and the latest campaign. “You evolve with every single competition. You learn something or the other.You win or you don’t win, but you always learn.”The medal was the culmination of a more comprehensive preparation programme, one that she believes made a tangible difference. Ahead of the Games, the Sports Authority of India (SAI), in coordination with the National Rifle Association of India (NRAI), organised two preparatory camps. The first, held in Aug, focused on fundamentals, while the Sept camp concentrated on fine-tuning and final preparations.The support structure, she says, was also stronger than before, with foreign coaching expertise and a larger team of support staff contributing to the preparations.An important part of that preparation was the presence of her personal coach, Anthony, an Olympic medallist from France. She received permission from the federation to have him join the national camp and accompany her to Japan, where he worked alongside national coaches and foreign coach Riccardo Filippelli.For her, the arrangement was about more than technical advice. A personal coach who has worked with an athlete over an extended period understands the individual beyond the shooting range, including their habits, temperament and response to pressure.“My personal coach might have seen my tantrums or might have seen a lot,” she says with a laugh. “He has seen various sides of me because I train with him a lot more than I do with my national coach.”She is particularly appreciative of the cooperation between the coaches, describing the atmosphere as one without ego or insecurity. Anthony, she adds, was equally conscious of respecting the national coaching structure.Her introduction to shooting began well before she took up skeet seriously. Growing up around firearms, she was familiar with the sport, and her father, Ratandeep Dhaliwal, encouraged her to learn how to use a weapon. At Mayo College Girls’ School in Ajmer, she participated in open-sight shooting competitions and school-level events.When she turned 13, her father suggested that she explore shotgun shooting. She initially tried trap, but it was an unexpected session at the skeet range that changed her trajectory.During a week at home to prepare for a state competition, her mentor, Amarjang Singh Sidhu, suggested that she try a station of skeet. She hit a couple of targets and immediately found herself drawn to the discipline.“I looked at my dad and said, ‘Papa, I think I want to do skeet.’ He was like, ‘Huh?’” she recalls.Her father discussed the decision with her grandfather, and by the following day, she had a skeet gun.“It turned out to be a great decision,” she says. While she remains close to several trap shooters, skeet is the discipline she finds more engaging. The experience reinforced a lesson she considers fundamental to sporting success: an athlete must enjoy what they do.Behind the medals, however, lies a challenge that is often overlooked: the financial demands of competitive shooting.Shotgun shooting, she explains, can be particularly expensive, making financial stability and institutional support crucial for aspiring athletes. Equipment, training and travel can place a substantial burden on families, while sponsorships often arrive only after an athlete has established a record.Despite having competed at the previous Asian Games, she says she relied on her family to fund her development for years, even while working with internationally accomplished coaches, fitness professionals and sports psychologists.She is grateful for the backing, but is equally conscious of the sacrifices that preceded it. Her father had travelled with her to competitions and camps, both in India and abroad. This year, however, he stepped back from travelling because her grandparents were unwell and needed family support.“I said, for me and for my mental sanity, it’s just better that you are at home with my grandparents. And I’m fine,” she says, drawing on the independence she developed during her years at boarding school.For young shooters, she believes, understanding the financial realities of the sport is as important as recognising their own potential.Parinaaz’s preparation has evolved beyond technique and equipment. Over the past three years, she has worked extensively on fitness and the technical aspects of her shooting, while also consulting a sports psychologist based in the UK.At the elite level, she believes, every component matters. “You cannot leave anything unattended at all,” she said.One incident from the World Cup in Lonato, Italy, illustrates the importance she places on mental preparation. After the first four rounds, she was uncertain about her standing and found herself worrying about the competition. Anthony responded by taking her out for dinner rather than allowing her anxiety to dominate the evening.She was initially concerned about losing sleep ahead of the following morning’s round. Her coach, however, believed that continuing to dwell on the competition would be counterproductive.The evening continued with a walk by the lake and gelato, helping her shift her attention away from the scoreboard and reconnect with the reasons she had taken up shooting.Anthony, she said, believes strongly in maintaining balance and reminding athletes why they compete in the first place.The next day, she shot a perfect round of 25, her best of the competition, which helped her reach a shoot-off.“These are the small things that coaches with experience can teach you,” she said.At the Asian Games, the women's team faced a difficult opening day, but the athletes concentrated on their individual routines rather than becoming distracted by the collective result.Skeet may have a team component, but the discipline demands individual accountability. Each shooter must execute their own process, manage pressure and remain focused on the target in front of them.The team's positive atmosphere helped them persevere, while the men's skeet team also produced a strong finish. India ultimately returned with medals in both the men's and women's team events.For her, the result reflected not only individual ability but also the value of a supportive environment in which athletes and coaches worked towards a common objective.She also believes India's development in skeet coaching needs greater attention. While the country has several accomplished coaches in trap, she sees a relative shortage of experienced specialists in skeet. International coaches, despite their high fees, can offer technical knowledge and an understanding of competitive pressure acquired through years at the highest level.At the same time, she acknowledges that being an accomplished shooter does not automatically make someone an accomplished coach. Coaching, she says, is a discipline in itself.Looking ahead, she intends to continue building on the progress she has made through competition experience, technical refinement and mental preparation. Her latest Asian Games performance is a milestone, but not the end of the journey.For a shooter whose career began with a spontaneous decision at 13, the larger lesson remains remarkably simple: excellence comes from getting the fundamentals right, learning from every competition and finding the people who help you become better.And perhaps that is what defines Parinaaz’s journey best. The targets may be fleeting, but the work behind each shot is anything but.
Article Summary: Parinaaz Dhaliwal won a bronze medal in the women's skeet team event at the Asian Games 2026 at Aichi-Nagoya in Japan. She believes experience, the right coaching environment and an unwavering support system have helped her take significant strides forward. She is grateful for the backing, but equally conscious of the sacrifices that preceded it.

MUMBAI: In a major setback for Mumbai at the start of the Ranji Trophy season, their newly appointed vice-captain Ayush Mhatre has suffered a recurrence of his right hamstring injury and has been ruled out for a month. The setback means the young opener is set to miss Mumbai’s remaining three matches of the first leg of the Ranji Trophy, TOI has learnt.The recurrence is a big blow for Mhatre, who was recently named Siddhesh Lad’s deputy for the Ranji Trophy by the Mumbai selectors.The top-order batter had earlier suffered a hamstring injury while playing for Chennai Super Kings (CSK), which ruled him out of the second half of IPL 2026. He was subsequently out of action for almost five months, missing the T20 Mumbai tournament in June, India A’s tour of Sri Lanka and the Duleep Trophy in August.Mhatre sustained the injury after scoring 48 on the opening day of Mumbai’s first-innings effort against Chandigarh at the Wankhede Stadium. He did not take the field on the second and third days of the Ranji Trophy 2026-27 match. The 19-year-old underwent scans on Monday, while substitute Suved Parkar fielded in his place.At the time of his injury during IPL 2026, Mhatre was CSK’s leading run-scorer in the tournament, with 201 runs in six innings at a strike rate of 177.87.Mhatre had undergone rehabilitation at the Centre of Excellence (CoE) in Bengaluru. The Mumbai Cricket Association’s (MCA) physio cleared him to return to the Ranji Trophy after he featured in the final round of the Kanga League, scoring 25 for Sainath Cricket Club in a ‘B’ Division match.His latest injury could open the door for in-form Kolkata Knight Riders opener Angkrish Raghuvanshi, 22, to earn a call-up for Mumbai’s next Ranji Trophy match against Himachal Pradesh in Bilaspur from October 18 to 21. Raghuvanshi has struck back-to-back double centuries, scoring 203 and 201 for the Rest of India Under-23 team against Tamil Nadu in Chennai and for the Mumbai Under-23 side against Bengal in Kolkata on Tuesday, respectively.At Mumbai’s pre-season press conference, Mhatre had spoken about his preparations following a lengthy injury layoff. With captain Siddhesh Lad seated beside him, he said, "I was in the nets for three weeks. So, the preparation is going really well. And I have got some games also in the CoE. We (the Mumbai team) played at MCA-BKC also. So, it was really good for us to spend some time on the ground. So, we are well prepared. "
Article Summary: Ayush Mhatre has suffered a recurrence of his right hamstring injury. The 19-year-old is set to miss Mumbai's remaining three matches of the first leg of the Ranji Trophy. The top-order batter had earlier suffered a hamstring injury while playing for Chennai Super Kings (CSK), which ruled him out of the second half of IPL 2026.

Article Title: Pink ball in day Tests? Shaun Pollock’s bold idea to tackle bad light sparks debate
Article Text:
L-R: Shaun Pollock; and South African batters at stumps on Day 4 of first Test vs Australia in Durban.

‘You cannot play Test cricket past bad light time’

Pollock questions whether teams would agree in a high-stakes Test

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Ashwell Prince backs tradition of red-ball cricket

Former South Africa all-rounder Shaun Pollock has called for the use of pink balls in traditional daytime Test matches to minimise the loss of playing time due to bad light, reigniting the debate over whether cricket should rethink its long-standing red-ball convention.Pollock's suggestion comes after persistent weather interruptions disrupted the ongoing first Test between South Africa and Australia at Kingsmead in Durban, with only 221 of the scheduled 270 overs bowled across the first three days. The match finally enjoyed an extended spell of uninterrupted sunshine on Monday, but South Africa were left facing a daunting target of 421 after Australia's second-innings declaration.At stumps on Day 4, the hosts were struggling at 102/4, with Aiden Markram unbeaten on 45 and Australia firmly in control heading into the final day.The International Cricket Council (ICC) has recently permitted the use of pink balls in daytime Test matches on a trial basis, provided both captains agree to the arrangement before the game. Once approved, the pink ball must be used throughout the match, with no provision to switch back to the traditional red ball.Pollock believes the option deserves serious consideration, particularly when poor light threatens to eat into valuable playing time."I am not saying for one moment that we should have used the pink ball and played a day-night game," Pollock told Fox Sports."I just believed we should have used the pink ball for the day game. It is not irrelevant because if you use the red ball, all of a sudden you cannot play Test cricket past bad light time, but if you use the pink one, you can," he said.The former Proteas star's argument centres on the visibility advantage offered by the pink ball, potentially allowing umpires to keep play going in conditions when a red ball would no longer be considered safe to use.With Test cricket increasingly under pressure to maximise playing time, Pollock's proposal raises a question about whether tradition should take precedence when weather threatens to affect the outcome of a match.Pollock also questioned whether teams would be willing to accept the change when the stakes are particularly high, suggesting that a theoretical agreement could become more complicated when a major result is on the line.“If this was a final or a game where you had to win to enter the World Test Championship final and it was 1-all in the series, and Australia was playing South Africa and you tell them, ‘Let’s use the pink ball because we are going to lose 100 overs to bad light’ do you think they would agree or not agree?” he questioned.His comments highlight a potential obstacle to the ICC's trial: the requirement for both captains to agree before the match. Even if the pink ball could help reduce weather-related interruptions, teams may be reluctant to adopt a format with which they have limited experience.South Africa senior assistant coach Ashwell Prince, however, remains firmly in favour of the traditional red ball for daytime Tests, arguing that differences in experience between teams could make agreement difficult.“For me, outside of a day-night Test, it has got to be a red ball. I think, obviously some nations have played a lot more pink ball cricket than others and so, therefore, to get both captains to agree is always going to be a challenge.“To get both captains to agree to that, some teams will feel that they simply do not have enough experience of it, so, I think it would be very difficult to get both captains to agree. But for me, you know, Test matches are the red ball," said Prince.The contrasting views underline the challenge facing cricket authorities as they consider ways to protect playing time without compromising the character of the longest format.
Article Summary: Former South Africa all-rounder Shaun Pollock has called for the use of pink balls in traditional daytime Test matches to minimise loss of playing time due to bad light. Pollock's suggestion comes after persistent weather interruptions disrupted the ongoing first Test between South Africa and Australia at Kingsmead in Durban. South Africa were struggling at 102/4, with Aiden Markram unbeaten on 45 and Australia firmly in control heading into the final day.

Article Title: ‘I am up for the challenge’: Tushar Deshpande after 5-17, including hat-trick, in Ranji Trophy opener
Article Text:
Tushar Deshpande (Pic credit: X)

MUMBAI: Over the years, the Wankhede Stadium has seen plenty of memorable batting and bowling performances in First-Class cricket. Mumbai pacer Tushar Deshpande 's devastating spell against Chandigarh, that saw him take five for 17 in seven fiery overs including a hat-trick, and one wicket in the only over that he bowled in the second innings, on Day two of their Elite Ranji Trophy Group D opening match will rank right amongst the best.Hurting clearly after being overlooked for India A's upcoming tour of New Zealand, Deshpande, bending his back to extract as much life from the juicy, fresh Wankhede track as was possible, fired on all cylinders, ripping out the heart of Chandigarh's batting like knife going through melting butter. Generating healthy pace, the 'Kalyan Express' was all over Chandigarh's batters on Monday.The hat-trick, which included the wickets of Arjun Azad (top-edged a hook to Sylvester D’Souza at long leg), Shivam Bhambri (a superb away going delivery hit the top of off-stump) and Dipender Kush (a fine catch by Yashasvi Jaiswal at first slip) was the icing on the cake for Deshpande, who celebrated his 50th first-class match in grand fashion."It's my 50th first class match today. So it was just in my mind that I wanted to make it special, but it wasn't like a hat-trick and all that, but I was going to give my 100% today. And when I was batting, there were some patches on the wicket where the ball was seeming a bit. So, my only focus was to bowl maximum balls in the right area and it paid dividends today," Deshpande told reporters after the day's play.Deshpande's spirited performance with the ball came after he had a decent outing with the bat on a hot day, after he had stroked a 47-ball 44, which included four fours and two sixes, to reiterate his utility with the bat.Asked if it was a challenging task to give it all with the ball after batting for that long a while earlier, Deshpande bared his ambitions to be considered a genuine allrounder for India in Test cricket."I think it was challenging (to bowl in this heat after batting earlier). It was hot. But if I want to come in the all-rounder category, or I have to show that I can bat, I have to do this thing. So, it's kind of hard work. Or you can say putting in the hard yards with my batting as well. So, yes, I am up for the challenge," he stressed.With national selector SS Das watching Deshpande's exploits from the MCA President's Box, was it a statement performance? "You can call it whatever you want, but the job is half done. We have just put them to follow on, but we have to come again tomorrow, bowl in the right areas and finish the job as early as possible," a focused-looking Deshpande, who took 134 wickets in 49 matches@28.67, with five wicket hauls in first-class match before this match, asserted.Was it disappointing to not be picked for the 'shadow tour' to New Zealand, and did it provide the 'Kalyan Express' with added motivation? "There is always motivation to play Test cricket for India, no matter if I am selected for India A or not. I thought for a day about that, but I have always said that I want to chase performance, not selection. So, I came back to Wankhede again, reset and do my process and bowl again," Deshpande said.Talking about the hat-trick ball, Deshpande, crediting Jaiswal for the fine grab, said, “I want to bowl my best ball, no matter what. I think it was my day. He could have just missed it or would have been beaten by it, but he nicked it to Jaiswal, who took a brilliant catch."Rating his sizzling performance as 'one of the best,' (his best fist class show is six for 70) Deshpande, while elaborating his second hat-trick ball, which was a 'Jaffa,' said, "If you saw, it was a top of the off-stump ball. And for a new batter to get such a ball, it's like a nightmare. As I said, I was just looking to bowl my best balls. And he got out on that."While it's his maiden first-class hat-trick, the 31-year-old Deshpande has achieved the feat earlier in his cricketing career. "I think I've picked (a hat-trick) right from school. I think I've picked a couple of hat-tricks at the club level, one at a summer camp, one in Mushtaq Ali, and one in KSCA Invitational. And now, the first in the Ranji Trophy," he said fondly.While one is used to see him bowl at speeds of around 140 kmph in the IPL, Monday's spell could be the fastest Deshpande has bowled in first-class cricket."I don't know about the speed in the match. But yes, recently when I was playing for India A (against Australia A), I was bowling at about 140s in every style with the red ball. I think it's not always the speed with the red ball. It's about the situation which you come to bowl in. It's not like T20 cricket, that I have to bowl just four overs. I have to bowl throughout the day. So, whatever the situation is, I look at what I can do the best. And accordingly increase or modify my speeds.Having batted well earlier on the same pitch, which had something to offer to the fast bowlers, Deshpande had a fair idea of how to utilise that knowledge in his bowling. "There were some patches in the middle of the grass. The ball was kicking a little bit. And as everyone knows, if you bowl in good areas, fast bowlers and spinners get a little bit of help. So, that help was there, and I thought it would be of maximum use today,” the allrounder explained.Getting off to the perfect start for the season, Deshpande hasn't set any goal for now. "No, I don't keep any number of goals. I just play game by game, do my best every day. And that's how I have been," he said, matter of factly.Meanwhile, pacer Sylvester D’Souza was fined 20% of his match fee for showing dissent against an umpiring decision.
Article Summary: Mumbai pacer Tushar Deshpande took five for 17 in seven fiery overs including a hat-trick, and one wicket in the only over that he bowled in the second innings. The 'Kalyan Express' took 134 wickets in 49 matches@28.67, with five wicket hauls in first-class match before this match. He had stroked a 47-ball 44, which included four fours and two sixes.

However, Sudharsan’s stay at the crease lasted for only 10 balls. He was cleaned up by debutant pacer Chetan Sharma for just 3 runs. Narayan Jagadeesan (55: 99b, 5x4, 1x6) and Pradosh Ranjan Paul (58: 101b, 5x4) then slammed half-centuries each to give the innings stability.The left-right combination of Pradosh and Jagadeesan added 104 runs for the second wicket before Ajay Singh Kukna struck twice in a short span of four overs to get rid of both of them.First he forced Jagadeesan to loft the ball straight to long-off fielder Rohan Rajbhar as the wicketkeeper-batter failed to judge the flight. Later he bowled Pradosh round his legs.Baba Indrajith and C Andre Siddarth then tried to get things back on track with a 46-run stand. Just when it looked TN would end the day without any further damage, part-time off-spinner Rohan castled Indrajith, again round his legs as the ball turned sharply after pitching.At stumps, Andre Siddarth (21) and nightwatchman Sonu Yadav (0) were batting at the crease.Earlier, resuming on their overnight score of 286 for 4, Rajasthan squandered away the strong start and added just 77 runs to be all out for 363 in 115.3 overs.At one stage, the hosts were well placed at 347 for 5 and a total of 400-plus was on the cards. However, the hosts lost their last five wickets for the addition of only 16 runs.The star of the opening day, Karan Lamba, who was batting on 103, could not last long and was trapped in front of the wickets by TN medium-pacer Sonu Yadav for 113.The other overnight batter, Mahipal Lomror, completed his half-century before he was caught by substitute S Ajith Ram off Deepesh Devendran for 66 triggering a lower-order collapse.Teenage pace sensation Deepesh bagged 3-89 on his First-Class debut after going wicketless on Sunday.“I didn’t feel bad for not picking any wicket in my first 19 overs. Even then, the coaches backed me, saying you bowl giving your full effort, don’t feel bad about leaking runs. So I did that. I gave full effort to see what happens. So this gave a very good result. I concentrated both on pace and accuracy,” an 18-year-old Deepesh told TOI after the day’s play.Rajasthan skipper Manav Suthar praised his inexperienced bowling attack for restricting the opponents.“Our bowlers really bowled well and didn’t concede many runs. The match is evenly balanced right now. If we manage to take a couple of wickets early tomorrow morning, we certainly have a chance of taking the first-innings lead,” said Suthar.Rajasthan 363 in 115.3 overs (Karan Lamba 113, Mahipal Lomror 66, Sumit Godara 49; Saravana Kumar 3-68, Deepesh Devendran 3-89, Washington Sundar 2-58). Tamil Nadu 167/4 in 50 overs (Pradosh Ranjan Paul 58, Narayan Jagadeesan 55, C Andre Siddarth 21*; Ajay Singh Kukna 2-31).
Article Summary: Sai Sudharsan had a forgettable day as the four-day Rajasthan-Tamil Nadu Ranji Trophy match was evenly poised at the halfway stage. Tamil Nadu were 167 for 4 on Day 2 at the Sawai Mansingh Stadium here on Monday. The visitors still need 197 runs to take the first-innings lead.

Article Title: England batter Ollie Pope withdraws from Afghanistan T20 league draft amid concerns over Taliban’s treatment of women
Article Text:
England's Ollie Pope during practice session Action Images via Reuters/Andrew Boyers

The debate over cricket and human rights

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

England batter Ollie Pope has withdrawn from the draft for the inaugural Afghanistan Premier League (APL), which is scheduled to take place in the United Arab Emirates later this year. His decision comes amid debate over whether English cricketers should participate in the competition because of the Taliban’s treatment of women and girls in Afghanistan.Pope was expected to be the only centrally contracted England player in the draft. However, his withdrawal was understood to be his own decision, rather than a direct result of discussions with England director of cricket Rob Key. Players need a No Objection Certificate (NOC) from the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) to participate in overseas leagues.“Legally it is hard to stop players going over and playing in these competitions,” Key told the Test Match Special podcast, as quoted by BBC. “It becomes a moral judgement and players have to be prepared to take the right moral stance.“Personally, and it is easy for me to say, I would not go and play. But it is down to the player to make that decision.”The ECB has refused to arrange bilateral series against Afghanistan since the Taliban returned to power in 2021. However, England continue to face Afghanistan in major international tournaments, including the World Cup and Champions Trophy.Key also expressed his opposition to the treatment of women in Afghanistan. “I don't agree with the way women have been treated in Afghanistan,” said Key. “The way things happen out there is not something I agree with so it is not something I would go and do.”Former England batter Dawid Malan, however, is among those entered in the APL draft, alongside Moeen Ali, James Vince and James Rew. Malan said players faced a difficult choice between personal beliefs and earning a living.“As a player it is tough because you have what is morally right and what is by the law,” Malan said, adding that players often needed their cricket boards to take a clear position.He also questioned why players were expected to make individual decisions when England continued to play Afghanistan in global tournaments.
Article Summary: Ollie Pope withdraws from Afghanistan Premier League draft. Decision comes amid debate over whether English cricketers should participate. Players need a No Objection Certificate (NOC) from the England and Wales Cricket Board. ECB has refused to arrange bilateral series against Afghanistan since Taliban returned to power in 2021.
