Article Title: 'It's like water to a thirsty person': Asian Games gold reignites women's hockey at grassroots
Article Text:
Image credit: Hockey India

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

KOLKATA: The Indian women’s hockey team’s Asian Games gold medal after a 44-year wait has done more than secure direct qualification for the Olympics.According to coaches who have nurtured generations of players across the country, the triumph has rekindled belief at the grassroots, and is destined to inspire a new generation of girls to take up the sport while validating decades of hard work in academies and training centres, far from the spotlight.Former India captain Pritam Siwach, who has been working as a coach for more than 25 years in Sonipat, Haryana, believes the impact of the victory extends well beyond the podium.“This victory has given women’s hockey a new lease of life. It is like giving water to a thirsty person. Winning gold after 44 years has ended a long drought and brought renewed energy to the sport,” she said, adding that the success has given women’s hockey the recognition it deserves after years of operating in the shadow of the men’s game.For coaches working at the grassroots level, the medal has become a powerful tool. Dasrath Mahato, the 69-year-old from Khunti in Jharkhand who discovered and mentored Nikki Pradhan, said every major success creates a ripple effect among young athletes.“When children see players returning home with medals, they start to believe they can do the same. It inspires them to work harder and pursue hockey seriously,” Mahato said.The success has also been celebrated by coaches who have worked in some of the country’s leading hockey centres. Madhya Pradesh Hockey Academy coach Vandana says achievements at the elite level invariably strengthen the grassroots ecosystem.“When a sport performs well at the top level, it benefits the grassroots. We are already seeing more academies and leagues being established for women, and success like this will only accelerate that growth,” said Vandana, who trained the likes of Sushila Chanu and Bichu Devi Kharibam.Former India goalkeeper and coach Edgar Mascarenhas, who worked extensively in Odisha, described the achievement as one of the biggest milestones in the history of Indian women’s hockey.“I watched every match and what impressed me most was their fighting spirit. Even in difficult situations, they never gave up,” said Mascarenhas.The direct Olympic qualification has also been highlighted as one of the competition’s biggest outcomes. Coaches unanimously agreed that avoiding the pressure of an additional qualification campaign allows the team to focus entirely on preparation for the Games.“This may actually be even more important than the gold medal itself,” said Siwach. “Now the players know they are going to the Olympics and can devote all their energy towards preparing for that challenge.”The impact has been felt in regions that have emerged as strong contributors to Indian women’s hockey. In Mizoram, where coach Miss Btei helped nurture internationals Lalremsiami and Lalthantluangi, interest in the sport continues to grow among young children.“The success of players from our state will encourage more youngsters to take up hockey. Children see what Lalremsiami has achieved and begin to believe they can follow the same path,” she said.According to Btei, players as young as nine or ten years old, are now entering the development pathway with the latest generation already benefiting from the visibility created by the national team’s success.For former India international and coach Ajit Lakra, the gold medal represents proof that India’s grassroots structures are delivering results.“These players came through the grassroots system and delivered a gold-medal performance that resonated across Asia. It shows young athletes that there is a pathway from the grassroots level to the international stage,” said Lakra, who coached Rutuja Dadaso Pisal.While they welcomed the growing number of opportunities for women, the coaches stressed the importance of greater investment in infrastructure, academies and player development programmes to sustain the momentum.Yet the overriding sentiment remains one of optimism. Whether in hockey strongholds like Jharkhand and Odisha, established academies in Madhya Pradesh or emerging centres like Mizoram, coaches see the medal as a catalyst for growth.
Article Summary: The Indian women's hockey team's Asian Games gold medal after a 44-year wait has done more than secure direct qualification for the Olympics. The triumph has rekindled belief at the grassroots, and is destined to inspire a new generation of girls to take up the sport.

Article Title: Cristiano Ronaldo shares untold Messi story, reveals he used to translate English for him at award ceremonies
Article Text:
Cristiano Ronaldo reveals he often translated English for Lionel Messi at award ceremonies, offering a glimpse into their respectful relationship beyond football’s legendary rivalry/ Image: Balland'or

Ronaldo recalls helping Messi at awards ceremonies

For nearly two decades, Messi and Ronaldo have shared award stages, collected countless trophies and dominated football’s biggest nights

Ronaldo still refuses to call Messi the greatest

Ronaldo’s retirement question adds urgency to the milestone

For 15 years, Cristiano Ronaldo and Lionel Messi shared football’s biggest stages, competing for trophies and individual honours while millions argued over which of them deserved the title of the greatest ever. Away from the spotlight, however, their relationship was friendlier than their rivalry suggested, with Ronaldo revealing that he even helped Messi understand English during awards ceremonies. The Portugal captain has now opened up about their mutual respect, although he remains unwilling to give up his claim to football’s ultimate crown.Speaking to CNN Portugal, the 41-year-old Al-Nassr forward recalled how he occasionally translated instructions for Messi when they appeared together at award ceremonies, offering a glimpse of their relationship away from the competition.“We shared the award stages for 15 years,” Ronaldo said.“And we always got along very well. I remember a time or two translating for him what they were saying in English, ‘Messi, you’re going to stay here’.”Ronaldo explained that he would help Messi understand what presenters wanted him to do, including when they told the Argentine that someone would ask him a question.“Afterwards, she’s going to ask you a question. And I would translate.The presenter would say to you: ‘We are going to do this’, and you would tell Messi: ‘Yes, very good’. And it was funny.He added that Messi had always treated him well despite their competing loyalties.“He always treated me well. Of course he defended his club and I, mine. He defended his national team and I, mine,” Ronaldo said.Their rivalry often appeared personal to supporters debating their respective achievements, but Ronaldo presented it as a healthy competition between two players determined to keep improving. He compared their relationship to that of Formula One greats Ayrton Senna and Alain Prost, whose rivalry helped define their sport.“I think there were years where he wanted to give everything and score, and so did I. It was a healthy rivalry, like the one they had maybe Ayrton Senna and Prost. I think we motivated each other,” he said.Their mutual respect has not changed Ronaldo’s position in the enduring debate over football’s greatest player, even though Messi holds advantages in several major categories, including World Cup success and Ballon d’Or awards, with eight to Ronaldo’s five.Ronaldo accepts that individual supporters will naturally favour different players, but he draws a clear distinction between personal preference and questioning his own ability.“Personal preference is one thing, saying this, this, this… prefer Messi, Pelé, or Maradona. I understand that and I respect it,” he said.“But saying that Cristiano isn’t complete is a lie.”Ronaldo’s argument rests heavily on his extraordinary goalscoring record, with the forward having scored 980 goals across 1,337 professional appearances for club and country. He believes his performances still receive insufficient recognition, particularly as discussion increasingly centres on whether he can reach 1,000 career goals.“People are not appreciating my current form, my goals,” Ronaldo said.“They are more concerned with saying that there are 85 goals left, 85 goals to go… But I don’t like that. I don’t like it.”He also made clear that reaching four figures would be an extraordinary achievement rather than something that determines his place in football history.“Things have to happen naturally. If I score 920 goals, 925, 930… I am the best in history, full stop,” he said. “Scoring goals, the numbers speak for themselves. So, I’m not going to sit here and say that I have to reach a thousand goals. If I reach it, fantastic.”The interview comes amid uncertainty over how much longer Ronaldo intends to continue playing, after he suggested last month that he would probably retire when the Saudi Pro League season ends next June. Asked about his long-term future, he has acknowledged that his motivation could change, making his remaining playing years difficult to predict.Ronaldo is now back with Al-Nassr after leaving Portugal’s national team camp during the October international break following a dispute with head coach Jorge Jesus. However, Portugal’s federation president and Jesus have since publicly expressed their desire to welcome him back, opening the possibility of a return during November’s international window, depending on the outcome of the disciplinary proceedings.Messi, meanwhile, has reportedly brought his Argentina international career to an end, with speculation also growing that he could retire altogether when the MLS season concludes with Inter Miami.Their careers are approaching their final chapters at different speeds, but Ronaldo’s comments show that his respect for Messi does not require him to surrender their rivalry. Even after 15 years of competing together, he continues to believe the numbers support his own claim, while leaving open the possibility of one more remarkable milestone before his playing days end.
Article Summary: Cristiano Ronaldo reveals he often translated English for Lionel Messi at award ceremonies, offering a glimpse into their respectful relationship. The Portugal captain has now opened up about their mutual respect, although he remains unwilling to give up his claim to football’s ultimate crown. Ronaldo compared their relationship to that of Formula One greats Ayrton Senna and Alain Prost.

Article Title: Former Brighton and Port Vale captain Doug Loft dies at 39 as tributes pour in from 9 heartbroken clubs
Article Text:
Former Port Vale and Brighton captain Doug Loft dies aged 39, as nine heartbroken clubs pay tribute to the respected midfielder and leader.

Loft made his mark at Port Vale after emerging at Brighton

Port Vale and former manager Micky Adams lead tributes

Brighton, Gillingham and Tonbridge Angels pay tribute

Doug Loft, the former Port Vale and Gillingham captain who spent more than a decade playing across English football, has died at the age of 39 following a medical emergency over the weekend. Tributes have poured in from the clubs he represented, with Port Vale remembering a leader whose commitment helped secure promotion and former manager Micky Adams recalling the pride Loft took in captaining the team.Loft began his senior career at non-League Hastings United before joining Brighton & Hove Albion in January 2006, shortly after his 20th birthday. He made 49 appearances for Brighton before moving to Port Vale in the summer of 2009, beginning a five-season spell that would become the defining chapter of his career.The versatile midfielder made 196 appearances for Port Vale, scoring 19 goals, and quickly became a favourite among supporters through his work rate and determination. He was named the club's Player of the Season for 2011-12 before being appointed captain ahead of the following campaign, when Vale secured promotion from League Two under Adams.Loft left Vale Park in 2014 to join Gillingham, where he continued his leadership role and made 70 appearances during two seasons in League One.His professional career also included spells at Colchester United, Shrewsbury Town and Dagenham & Redbridge, before he continued playing in non-League football with Billericay Town, Margate and Tonbridge Angels.He eventually retired from playing in 2023, having represented clubs across different levels of the English game.Port Vale confirmed Loft's death in a statement, remembering the former captain for his contribution to the club during five seasons in Burslem.“He will be remembered fondly by everyone at the club, not only for his achievements on the pitch but for the commitment and leadership he showed throughout his time in Burslem,” the club said.Vale added: “The thoughts and heartfelt condolences of everyone at Port Vale are with Doug’s family, friends, former team-mates and all those who knew him, at this incredibly sad time.”The club also confirmed that, with the family's blessing, it had requested permission from the English Football League for players to wear black armbands and observe a minute's silence before the upcoming match against Chesterfield.Speaking to the BBC, former manager Adams paid tribute to Loft's pride in representing Vale, recalling a player who took his responsibilities as captain seriously.“There was nobody more proud to be captain of the Vale,” Adams said.BBC Radio Stoke's Phil Bowers also recalled Loft's leadership during his five years at the club, noting that he captained the side during its promotion-winning 2012-13 campaign. Adams said Loft had led with “enthusiasm and endeavour”, while Bowers reported that he left in 2014 to move back south with his family.Brighton expressed their sadness following news of Loft's death, remembering a player who had represented the Seagulls before establishing himself at Port Vale.“Everyone at the Albion is devastated to hear the news of Doug Loft’s sudden passing at the age of 39,” the club wrote on social media. “Doug played 42 times for the club & will always be fondly remembered by fans & staff alike.”Gillingham, where Loft also served as captain, confirmed that the former midfielder had died following a medical emergency over the weekend.“The Football Club is absolutely devastated to announce the death of former Gills Captain, Doug Loft,” the club said. “Our thoughts and condolences are with Doug’s wife Laura, their children Freya and Amelie, along with his friends and family at this very difficult time.”Tonbridge Angels also paid tribute to Loft, describing him as “a true professional, a talented player and a wonderful person”, while sending their condolences to his wife, children and wider family.Billericay Town extended their “prayers, sincere condolences and sympathy” to Loft's loved ones, and Dagenham & Redbridge said they were “deeply saddened” by the passing of their former player.Loft is survived by his wife, Laura, and their two daughters, Freya and Amelie. As tributes continue from the clubs he represented, his legacy remains closely tied to the leadership he brought to Port Vale and the promotion-winning team he captained in 2012-13.Port Vale concluded their tribute with a message to their former captain: “Rest in peace, Doug.”

Modrić arrived when Swansea needed a fresh start

A difficult season forced Swansea to change course

Swansea Oh Swansea

Snoop Dogg, new investors and a wider rebuilding plan

Modrić has moved on from Madrid, but remains an elite footballer

When Luka Modrić bought into Swansea City in April 2025, the Welsh club needed more than a famous name to change its fortunes, with financial losses mounting, managerial uncertainty lingering and Premier League football feeling increasingly distant. Eighteen months later, Swansea are leading the Championship, attracting heavyweight investors and rebuilding their football operations. Modrić’s arrival was never going to fix everything overnight, but what has happened since suggests that a club which had lost its direction is beginning to find it again.Modrić became a minority investor and co-owner on April 14, 2025, joining American investors Andy Coleman, Brett Cravatt, Nigel Morris and Jason Cohen, who had bought out former majority owners Jason Levien and Steve Kaplan in November 2024. The new ownership group had inherited a club facing uncertainty on the pitch and considerable financial pressure, making the Croatian’s arrival part of a wider effort to restore ambition and international visibility.Swansea were sitting 12th in the Championship with 54 points when Modrić joined, after head coach Luke Williams had been dismissed in March and Alan Sheehan had taken temporary charge. The club had not played in the Premier League since relegation was confirmed on May 13, 2018, following a 2-1 defeat by Stoke City, ending a seven-year stay in the top flight.The financial position was equally difficult, with Swansea reporting a £15.2 million ($20 million) pre-tax loss for the financial year ending June 2024, although that represented an improvement on the £17.9 million ($23.6 million) deficit recorded the previous year. Turnover stood at £21.5 million ($28.3 million), while stadium and training-ground costs added to the pressures of competing in the Championship without a comparable redistribution agreement with the Premier League.In their financial statement, the board acknowledged that maintaining competitiveness in the division required continued support from the ownership group, which remained the club’s principal source of funding.Modrić brought something different from a conventional financial investor, combining the reputation of a Ballon d’Or winner with experience of elite football and a global profile that could help attract commercial partners and strengthen recruitment.“This is an exciting opportunity. Swansea has a strong identity, an incredible fanbase, and the ambition to compete at the highest level,” Modrić said when the investment was announced. “Playing at the highest level, I believe I can provide my experience to the club. My goal is to support the club's growth in a positive way and to help to build an exciting future.”Swansea described the investment as an endorsement of their ambitions, saying Modrić would help the club attract global attention and progress on and off the pitch.Modrić's arrival did not immediately produce a turnaround, as Swansea struggled during the opening months of the 2025-26 season and found themselves worryingly close to the relegation zone by November. The ownership group responded with a more analytical approach to decision-making, eventually appointing Vitor Matos, a former Liverpool development coach who had worked under Jürgen Klopp, as head coach.Matos introduced a more aggressive, high-running style that revived elements of the traditional Swansea approach to possession and movement, helping the side regain stability after their difficult start. The improvement was gradual rather than spectacular, but it gave the club a platform to approach the following season with greater confidence and a clearer footballing identityThat progress has become more obvious in 2026-27, with Swansea collecting 20 points from their first nine league matches following a 2-1 victory over Norwich City on October 10. Their record of six wins, two draws and one defeat has taken them to the top of the Championship, representing their strongest start to a league campaign since 2019-20.For a club that had spent years struggling to turn its ambition of returning to the Premier League into something tangible, the change in mood matters almost as much as the position in the table. Steve Carroll, editor of the fanzine, told reporters: “You can see the ambition and the ideas are there. People are talking about us in a positive way again.”Swansea's revival is not confined to the first team, with the ownership group pursuing commercial growth and infrastructure changes intended to leave the club in a stronger position for the long term. Rapper Snoop Dogg has joined the minority ownership group since Modrić's arrival, adding another globally recognised name to the club's commercial profile.A strategic partnership with Los Angeles-based Shamrock Capital followed in July 2026, bringing additional financial backing from an investment firm managing approximately £5.5 billion ($7.3 billion) in assets. The deal formed part of a broader attempt to attract capital and develop the club without diluting existing shareholders' stakes.Swansea have also strengthened their football operations, appointing former Crystal Palace staff member Ben Stevens as sporting director and partnering with Jamestown Analytics to modernise player recruitment. The club is negotiating to purchase the Swansea.com Stadium and Fairwood training facility outright from the local council, while seeking to restore its academy to Category One status by 2027.Further plans include fresh investment in the women's team and major LED improvements around the stadium for supporters. The challenge is turning these projects into sustainable progress, particularly because the financial accounts remain a warning against assuming that a better league position automatically means a healthier business.In April 2026, Swansea reported a record £21.6 million ($28.5 million) net loss for the financial year ending June 2025, highlighting the cost of the rebuilding programme. There has nevertheless been encouraging commercial movement, with chief executive Tom Gorringe reporting in August that revenue had increased by more than 25% during the 2025-26 cycle, rising from approximately £22 million ($29 million) to around £27.8 million ($36.7 million).While Swansea have been rebuilding, Modrić has undergone a major transition of his own without stepping away from the game. He left Real Madrid in the summer of 2025 after 13 seasons, having won 28 trophies, including six European Cups, four La Liga titles and two Copa del Rey trophies, while registering 43 goals and 95 assists in 597 appearances.His Madrid career also brought the 2018 Ballon d'Or, the Best FIFA Men's Player award and the UEFA Player of the Year honour, cementing his place among the most accomplished midfielders of his generation. He joined AC Milan on a free transfer in July 2025 and made 37 appearances during his first season before agreeing to a contract extension through June 2027.At 41, Modrić remains an active member of Croatia's national team and captained the country at his fifth World Cup in the summer of 2026, when Croatia were eliminated by Portugal in the round of 32. He scored against the Czech Republic in Croatia's Nations League campaign on September 26, and on October 11, he came off the bench to provide the assist for Adrien Rabiot's equaliser in Milan's 1-1 draw with Sassuolo.His continued playing career gives Swansea a connection to a footballer who understands the demands of elite competition from the inside, rather than simply lending his name to an ownership announcement. The club still have financial challenges to overcome, and nine Championship matches are not enough to guarantee promotion, but the combination of better results, fresh investment and a clearer footballing plan has changed the conversation around Swansea.Modrić arrived when the club needed a fresh start, and the progress since then suggests that his first move into ownership has coincided with a more convincing direction for the Swans.
Article Summary: Luka Modrić became a minority investor and co-owner of Swansea City on April 14, 2025. The Croatian joined American investors Andy Coleman, Brett Cravatt, Nigel Morris and Jason Cohen, who had bought out former majority owners Jason Levien and Steve Kaplan in November 2024. Swansea reported a £15.2 million pre-tax loss for the financial year ending June 2024, although that represented an improvement on the £17.9 million deficit recorded the previous year.
